NOAA CPC official synopsis

Issued 8 October 2026 · next update 12 November 2026

El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027 (remaining greater than an 83% chance).

El Niño strengthened further last month, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding +4.0°C in portions of the eastern equatorial Pacific [Fig. 1] . Most Niño indices increased in the past month, reaching +2.1°C in Niño 3.4, +3.0°C in Niño 3, and +3.9°C in Niño 1+2 [Fig. 2] . The equatorial subsurface temperature index (average from 180°-100°W) was well above average [Fig. 3] , reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline. Subsurface temperatures remained in excess of +10.0°C at depth in the eastern Pacific Ocean [Fig. 4] . Low-level westerly wind anomalies and upper-level easterly wind anomalies stretched from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific. Enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific, while anomalies remained suppressed over Indonesia [Fig. 5] . The traditional and equatorial Southern Oscillation indices were significantly negative. Collectively, the coupled ocean-atmosphere system reflected a strengthening El Niño.

The CPC Official ENSO outlook , which synthesizes multiple models from North America and abroad, indicates El Niño will continue to strengthen through the end of the year [Figs. 6 -7 -8] . Chances remain high for a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a 3-month RONI value ): the chance is 54% for September-November, 83% for October-December, and 70% for November-January. With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed (see CPC outlooks for probabilities of seasonal anomalies). In summary, El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027 (remaining greater than an 83% chance).

Footprints are deliberately coarse boxes. A teleconnection is a shift in a seasonal probability distribution over a broad region, and a precise polygon would claim a spatial resolution the underlying composites do not have. Nothing here is a forecast for a specific place or date: it is a hazard outlook built from historical composites, and the caveats in the impacts section apply to every line of it.

This is the one panel in the system where a forecast it made is scored against an outcome in the same season. The Atlantic suppression and the east Pacific enhancement are the two most reliable seasonal signals El Niño has, and they are being tested here in public rather than asserted. About 96 per cent of a normal season's energy has fallen by this date, so the comparison has that much of a season behind it.

On stopping a hurricane: it is not possible. Project STORMFURY seeded eyewalls with silver iodide from 1962 to 1983 and was abandoned because the changes it produced could not be separated from natural eyewall replacement, and because mature hurricanes carry far too little supercooled water for seeding to work at all. A Category 4 releases on the order of 1019 joules a day as latent heat, several hundred times world electricity generation. What can be delivered is lead time, and the tracks above are four days of it.

Project STORMFURY, recreated

The 1962-83 hurricane modification experiment, rebuilt as a decision procedure and run against the storms that are live right now. Three parts, kept separate because they failed differently: the mechanism, the trigger, and the measurement.

2 of 2 live storms fail STORMFURY's own criteria. Every one of them fails on supercooled water, which is the criterion no hurricane has ever passed and the reason the programme ended.

TRIGGER

the seeding agent needs supercooled liquid water and hurricane eyewalls are already glaciated at seeding altitude. Nothing to freeze, so the mechanism never starts. Willoughby et al., Bull. Am. Meteorol. Soc., 1985.

MAGNITUDE

across 37 natural eyewall expansions in 13 hurricanes this season, conserving angular momentum predicted a mean 28.0% wind drop and the storms actually gave up 4.3%, overstating it 6.5-fold. A hurricane is fed high-momentum air continuously, so a closed-system argument is an upper bound, not a forecast. STORMFURY's predicted effect came from that same calculation.

DETECTION

25 of 300 unseeded hurricane intervals this season weakened by at least the 31% STORMFURY claimed for Debbie, and 56 moved that far in one direction or the other. An effect that size is indistinguishable from what hurricanes do untouched, which is what closed the programme.

The mechanism, computed

Seeding was supposed to build a new eyewall further out. Air arriving at a larger radius with the same absolute angular momentum turns more slowly, so the wind falls - and the arithmetic (M = rv + fr²/2) genuinely predicts a drop about the size STORMFURY reported. That part was never wrong.

What real eyewalls actually do

Hurricanes relocate their own eyewalls, unaided, several times a season. That gives a live test of the prediction above: take every natural expansion in a hurricane this season, ask what conserving angular momentum says the wind should become, and compare it with the wind the storm actually had six hours later.

Angular momentum predictedWhat the hurricane actually didWind before the eyewall moved (reference)

The prediction is consistently far too strong. A hurricane is not a spinning-down flywheel - it is fed high-momentum air continuously through the inflow, and the vortex restores itself while the eyewall moves. A closed-system momentum argument is an upper bound, not a forecast, and STORMFURY's expected effect came from exactly that calculation.

Why nobody could have told

The claimed result for Debbie was a 31% wind reduction. This is every 24-hour intensity change in every unseeded hurricane this season, on the same axis. An effect that has to be picked out of this distribution, from a sample of four storms, was never going to be separable from what hurricanes do on their own.

Would it even have been allowed to fly?

STORMFURY could not seed whatever it liked. Its own operating rules are checked here against each live storm - including the one rule no hurricane has ever passed.

Table view — STORMFURY criteria against live storms
StormIntensityCriterionVerdictDetail
Cempaka60 ktWithin aircraft rangeFail12,862 km from Lakeland, Florida, beyond the 2,040 km operational radius assumed here
Cempaka60 ktCoherent eyewallFail60 kt is below the 64 kt hurricane threshold; there is no closed eyewall to relocate
Cempaka60 ktClear of land for 24 hPassofficial track stays 942 km off the coast; no ensemble on file, so this is the deterministic track alone
Cempaka60 ktSupercooled water to seedFailHurricane eyewall updrafts are largely glaciated by the time they reach those temperatures. Warm-rain coalescence removes liquid water below the freezing level efficiently enough that little survives to be supercooled, leaving the seeding agent with nearly nothing to act on. The trigger is absent. The mechanism cannot start.
Pena45 ktWithin aircraft rangeFail7,540 km from Lakeland, Florida, beyond the 2,040 km operational radius assumed here
Pena45 ktCoherent eyewallFail45 kt is below the 64 kt hurricane threshold; there is no closed eyewall to relocate
Pena45 ktClear of land for 24 hPass0% of 31 tracks come within 80 km of land inside 24 h (rule: at most 10%); official track's closest approach 835 km
Pena45 ktSupercooled water to seedFailHurricane eyewall updrafts are largely glaciated by the time they reach those temperatures. Warm-rain coalescence removes liquid water below the freezing level efficiently enough that little survives to be supercooled, leaving the seeding agent with nearly nothing to act on. The trigger is absent. The mechanism cannot start.

The record

Table view — Storms STORMFURY seeded
StormYearDatesClaimedWhat it means
Esther1961September 1961about 10 per centFlown before STORMFURY formally existed, as the proof of concept that got the programme funded.
Beulah1963August 1963eyewall dissipated and reformed further outThe first run missed the target area entirely. The second produced the reformation the hypothesis predicted, which is also what an unseeded eyewall replacement looks like.
Debbie196918 and 20 August 196931 per cent, then 15 per centThe showcase: five seedings on each of two days. These are the numbers the programme is remembered for, and the ones the natural replacement cycle later explained without any silver iodide.
Ginger1971September 1971no measurable effectA large, diffuse storm with no coherent eyewall to move. It was seeded because it was what was available, which is itself a statement about how rarely the criteria above are met.

Four storms in twenty-one years, because the criteria above are almost never met at once. The seeding layer the hypothesis needed sits between 5.0 and 7.5 km, about 2.5 km deep, above a freezing level near 4.4 km - and the observation that closed the programme is that there is almost no supercooled water up there to freeze. Willoughby et al., Bull. Am. Meteorol. Soc., 1985

Formally ended in 1983. By then the natural eyewall replacement cycle had removed the evidence, the microphysics had removed the mechanism, and a move to the west Pacific in search of storms far from land had run into the problem that other nations' storms are not available to be experimented on.

What it did buy: Twenty years of research aircraft inside hurricanes. The eyewall replacement cycle, the modern understanding of hurricane structure, and the reconnaissance programme that still flies are all products of STORMFURY's observing arm. The measurement outlived the experiment it was built to serve. The deliverable from all of this is lead time, and the tracks and the forecast panels above are what lead time looks like.

The map

Open the El Niño Map → From the whole planet down to a single street, on Esri's street, satellite and terrain maps, with Google's own map, satellite view and Street View of any point on request. Over them go this tracker's El Niño composites for September to November, the season now: what the El Niño seasons since 1979 did to rainfall and temperature against the ordinary ones. Today's sea surface temperature anomaly and the last three days' floods come from NASA, and the documented impact regions are a tick away, solid where this event puts them in play.

  • Tap anywhere for what the El Niño seasons since 1979 did there, season by season, and whether the record can tell it from an ordinary year.
  • The documented effects whose regions take in the point, marked in play or on the watch list for this event.
  • Today's ocean temperature anomaly and flood class at that spot, read from NASA's own tiles, while those layers are on.
  • Google's map, satellite view and Street View of the point, and links that open it in Google Maps and Google Earth.

Where it lands

Every other tier here is about the Pacific. This one is about a point on the ground. The atlas holds what the El Niño events since 1979 actually did at each cell of the world - rainfall against an ordinary year, and surface temperature - and resolves a click to the nearest of 7,342 named places.

Open the interactive atlas → Drag to pan, scroll or use the buttons to zoom, click anywhere for the local record.

  • Composited per season over the El Niño events since 1979 in which RONI reached +1.0, against the neutral years (RONI inside +/-0.5): DJF 9 events (23 months) against 18 neutral years, |t| 2.31; MAM 6 events (10 months) against 33 neutral years, |t| 2.57; JJA 4 events (9 months) against 33 neutral years, |t| 3.18; SON 10 events (26 months) against 20 neutral years, |t| 2.26.
  • Each event counts once and each neutral year once, because the months inside one event are not independent. A cell is called wetter or drier only where Welch's t passes the 95% two-sided point of Student's t for its season's sample - the |t| quoted with each season. Everywhere else the record does not separate the event from an ordinary year, and the page says so rather than colouring it in.
  • The El Niño under way when the grids were built (2026) is not in the sample: the composite is what past events did.
  • The composite is what has happened in past events, not a forecast for this one. The forecast tier is the one that forecasts.

A verdict of 'no clear signal' is a measurement, not a gap: across that season's El Niños and neutral years, the record does not separate the two at that place. A temperature in parentheses does not pass the same test as the rainfall beside it: the sign is the composite's, the size is inside the noise.

The season shown is the one the rainfall record is most sure about at that place, which is not always the one the event peaks in: Jakarta's strongest signal is the June-to-August dry season, not the December monsoon, which is why El Niño fire years there are counted in the middle of the year.

Fortaleza is the one to read twice: the Nordeste drought is a textbook El Niño teleconnection, and the composite has it at -41% of normal in December to February - yet across 9 events its t of -1.86 does not reach the 2.31 that season's sample needs. The sign is right and the sample is not big enough to say so. Calling that a drought signal is the most common way a composite like this gets misused.

Read the percentages against the millimetres beside them. Los Angeles composites at +63% of normal in September to November, which sounds large and is 0.3 mm a day on top of an ordinary 0.5: the percentage is large because the season is dry there, not because the anomaly is.

Where the anomaly actually is

Daily OISST v2.1 sea-surface temperature anomaly for 2026-11-05, NOAA’s preliminary analysis (the final replaces it about two weeks on), on a half-degree sample of the quarter-degree analysis, against its 1971–2000 climatology. The four Niño boxes are drawn in their real positions with their area-weighted means, so the shape of the anomaly can be compared against the index it produces. The eastern edge of the 28 °C warm pool on the equator sits at 92W; in a neutral year it is near 180.

The four Niño boxes each day, on the Pacific map’s own half-degree cells: NOAA’s final analysis from 2026-07-25 to 2026-10-22, then NOAA’s preliminary analysis from 2026-10-23 to 2026-11-05. On the 14 days both analyses carry, the final runs 0.03 °C cooler than the preliminary in Niño 3.4 on average, and differs by up to 0.11 °C on a day (0.24 °C in Niño 1+2): about how far the shaded days may yet move.

The Indian Ocean Dipole day by day

The Dipole Mode Index each day, the SST anomaly of the west pole (50–70E, 10S–10N) less that of the east pole (90–110E, 10S–0), each area-weighted on half-degree cells: NOAA’s final analysis from 2026-07-25 to 2026-10-22, then NOAA’s preliminary analysis from 2026-10-23 to 2026-11-05. The DMI is +0.90 °C on 5 Nov 2026, -0.27 °C on the week. The Bureau of Meteorology counts a DMI above +0.4 °C as a positive IOD value and one below -0.4 °C as a negative one, and eight weeks of either as an event. The anomalies are OISST’s own, against its 1971–2000 climatology: a warming common to both poles cancels in their difference, but a difference in their warming does not, so the DMI here can run apart from the Bureau’s own, whose thresholds these are. IOD events typically develop from about May, peak from August to October and break down when the Australian monsoon arrives at the end of the southern spring, so a value past a threshold from December to April seldom marks one. On the 14 days both analyses carry, the final runs 0.06 °C higher than the preliminary in the DMI on average, and differs by up to 0.40 °C on a day: about how far the shaded days may yet move.

The thermocline, in three dimensions

Depth of the 20 °C isotherm across the TAO/TRITON array, as of 2026-11-01 6 days behind. Longitude runs west to east, latitude across, and the surface height is depth, so the sheet you are looking at is the top of the cold water. Colour is the anomaly against this mooring's own climatology for the calendar month. The east-west tilt along the equator is -11 m on this daily array; a neutral Pacific runs near 100 m, and a strong event flattens it. The cross-section below quotes the tilt between the same moorings from their monthly profiles, so the two numbers are two measurements of one quantity. Drag to rotate. Use the buttons for fixed views.

The thermocline in cross-section

Equatorial Pacific temperature against depth, 2026-10, from the TAO/TRITON moorings. This is the mechanism rather than the symptom: the surface warming that the indices measure is what happens after this slope relaxes. The 20 °C isotherm lies at 140 m at the west end of the basin (165E and 180) and 141 m at the east end (110W and 95W), a tilt of -1 m across the basin. A neutral Pacific runs near 100 m of tilt and a mature El Niño flattens it. The heavy line is the 20 °C isotherm, the conventional marker for the centre of the thermocline.

Is the atmosphere coupled to the ocean?

Every index is re-signed so that positive means El Niño-like, whatever its native convention, and standardised against its own calendar month. A warm ocean with a silent atmosphere is the 2014 failure mode, which is why these are reported separately from SST rather than blended into it.

The Southern Oscillation Index day by day

The Southern Oscillation Index day by day on the Bureau of Meteorology’s definition, Troup’s, as the Queensland Government’s LongPaddock works it out from each day’s Tahiti and Darwin pressures, 2026-07-10 to 2026-11-06. The Bureau’s own daily SOI data have been unavailable since January 2025, when Météo-France changed its Tahiti data service. The 30-day SOI is -13.3 on 6 Nov 2026, the 90-day -16.7. The 30- and 90-day SOI are the means of the days’ values, as LongPaddock’s own are, none where a window lacks more than five days or more than three in a row; sustained values below -7 are El Niño-like and above +7 La Niña-like. Each day’s SOI is ten times the standardised Tahiti less Darwin pressure difference, against 1933–1992, so CPC’s monthly SOI, a standard score, runs at about a tenth of the 30-day SOI; and the SOI keeps its own sign here, El Niño negative, where the coupling card signs every index El Niño-positive.

Westerly wind events day by day

Remote Sensing Systems’ Cross-Calibrated Multi-Platform (CCMP) 10 m winds, version 2.1 near real time, from NOAA PIFSC’s OceanWatch: an analysis of satellite radiometer and scatterometer winds over NCEP’s GFS, here at 06Z and 18Z on cells 2.25 degrees apart, 2026-05-10 to 2026-11-05. Westerly wind events are under way in the east region (180–150W, 5S–5N): 35.5 days above +2 m/s since 1 Oct 2026, peaking at +10.1 m/s on 12 Oct 2026 (longer than any in Harrison and Vecchi’s list); and in the central region (155E–180, 5S–5N): 8 days above +2 m/s since 28 Oct 2026, peaking at +5.0 m/s on 31 Oct 2026. Harrison and Vecchi’s 351 events of 1986–1995 lasted 32.5 days at most: a run longer is a sustained westerly anomaly more than a burst.

An event, as Harrison and Vecchi (1997) define one, is three days or more in which the 10 m zonal wind anomaly over one of their eight regions, cosine-weighted and smoothed by a three-point triangle filter on analyses 12 hours apart (half power at 2.75 days), stays above +2 m/s; an analysis is smoothed when the next one comes. Its centre is its largest smoothed value, its peak that value, its point peak the strongest cell in the region then, and its wind measure the time integral of its smoothed anomaly. Events in bordering regions centred within three days overlap, and count as the stronger. Against a monthly climatology an El Niño’s own westerly anomaly counts as well, so in a strong event the central and eastern regions’ runs can last weeks, the bursts within them showing in the chart and the Hovmoller. The anomalies are against CCMP version 2.0’s monthly means for 1991–2018 on the same cells, interpolated between the months’ middles. At 72 analysis times in 2016–2019 that both versions carry, the near-real-time product’s regional means differ from version 2.0’s by 0.20 m/s at most on average (in the north-west; 0.12 m/s at most in the equatorial regions), and by 0.19–0.51 m/s rms analysis by analysis. Against TAO’s daily winds at its seven reporting equatorial moorings, 165E to 95W, June to September 2026, its daily zonal wind correlates at 0.88–0.95 mooring by mooring. At 165E and 170W, where the wind was westerly on average, it ran 0.7 m/s less westerly than TAO’s; from 155W to 95W, 0.2 m/s more easterly. TAO measures at 4 m and CCMP is for 10 m, where a neutral log profile has the wind about 8% stronger: that leaves the eastern difference within 0.15 m/s and widens the western one to 0.9 m/s, so events’ peaks there may run low. The coupling card’s 850 hPa trades are CPC’s monthly indices, and the report’s westerly forcing counts months of the western one strongly westerly; these are the surface bursts themselves, days long, that force the downwelling Kelvin waves the Hovmoller card follows east.

Forecast

Three methods — analog ensemble, a nonlinear recharge oscillator and damped persistence — forecasting RONI, combined with weights taken from cross-validated hindcast over 77 years: analog 35%, recharge 37%, persistence 28%. The shaded fan is the 10th to 90th percentile; it is wide because the verification says it should be. Each probability is that of the likeliest season, on the one-decimal value CPC prints.

How much is that forecast worth?

Hindcast across 77 years with the verification year held out of every fit, so none of this is in-sample. Useful horizon at least 9 months, the longest lead scored. The right-hand panel is the spring predictability barrier as measured here, not as asserted from the literature: its weakest target seasons, MJJ, JJA, score 0.43 of correlation below the best.

Hazard outlook

An east-Pacific event. The coastal Peru/Ecuador flooding signal and Atlantic hurricane suppression are at their strongest in this flavour.

These are keyed to the PROJECTED RONI peak of +2.28 °C, not today's +1.97 °C. If the event underperforms the forecast, the lower-margin entries drop out first.

Hazard outlook from historical composites, not a forecast. ENSO shifts the odds; it does not decide the outcome, and vulnerability matters more than rainfall percentile.

Shifted odds from historical composites for a projected RONI peak of +2.28 °C with an east-Pacific structure. Not a forecast of any individual season, and not a substitute for your national meteorological service.

Maritime Continent

  • likelyIndonesia and MalaysiaJun 2026–Feb 2027, under way
    Suppressed rainfall; elevated peatland and forest fire risk

    Convection shifts east off the warm pool, leaving the archipelago under subsidence. The 1997-98 and 2015-16 events both produced severe haze episodes.

    Exposure Rice and palm systems, and transboundary haze affecting respiratory health across Singapore, Malaysia and southern Thailand.

  • likelyEastern AustraliaJun 2026–Feb 2027, under way
    Below-average rainfall, higher fire danger

    One of the oldest documented ENSO relationships. Strongly modulated by the Indian Ocean Dipole - a positive IOD compounds it, a negative one can cancel it.

    Exposure Wheat belt yields, water storage, and the summer bushfire season.

  • likelyPhilippinesSep 2026–Apr 2027, under way
    Rainfall deficit and delayed monsoon onset

    Reduced tropical cyclone landfalls but a genuine water deficit; typhoon tracks tend to shift east and recurve.

    Exposure Rice and maize irrigation, and hydropower supply on Luzon and Mindanao.

  • likelyPapua New Guinea highlandsAug 2026–Feb 2027, under way
    Drought and, at altitude, damaging frost

    Clear skies over high valleys allow radiative frost that destroys sweet potato, the staple crop, with no fallback.

    Exposure Subsistence farming communities with limited road access; 1997-98 required a large relief operation.

Africa

  • likelySouthern AfricaDec 2026–Mar 2027, ahead
    Rainfall failure during the main growing season

    The strongest and most consistent humanitarian teleconnection in the catalogue. It arrives precisely in the maize planting and grain-filling window across Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, Botswana and South Africa.

    Exposure Rain-fed maize for tens of millions of people, with regional price contagion when South African production falls.

  • likelyEquatorial East AfricaOct–Dec 2026, under way
    Enhanced short rains, flooding and landslides

    Kenya, southern Somalia, southeastern Ethiopia, Uganda and Tanzania. The sign is opposite to southern Africa and often surprises people expecting El Niño to mean drought everywhere.

    Exposure Displacement and damage to shelter and roads; flooding on top of existing drought recovery is a compounding failure, not an offsetting one.

  • likelyRift Valley fever risk, East AfricaNov 2026–Mar 2027, under way
    Outbreak conditions following heavy rain

    Flooding of dambo depressions hatches infected mosquito eggs. Major outbreaks followed the 1997-98 event in Kenya and Somalia.

    Exposure Livestock mortality and human infection, with export bans on livestock removing a primary income source.

  • likelyHighland malaria, East Africa and AndesDec 2026–May 2027, ahead
    Transmission at unusual altitude

    Warmer temperatures and standing water extend the vector range upslope into populations with little acquired immunity.

    Exposure Epidemic rather than endemic transmission, which health systems in those districts are not configured for.

  • likelyEthiopian highlands and SudanJun–Sep 2026, past
    Weak Kiremt rains

    The main Ethiopian growing rains fail before the enhanced short rains arrive, so a single event can deliver drought then flood within six months.

    Exposure Belg and Meher harvests, livestock condition, and Blue Nile inflow.

South America

  • likelyNorthern South AmericaDec 2026–Mar 2027, ahead
    Rainfall deficit

    Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana and northern Brazil sit under the descending branch through the wet season.

    Exposure Hydropower-dependent grids - Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador all draw most of their electricity from reservoirs - and Amazon river transport.

  • likelyNortheast BrazilFeb–May 2027, ahead
    Failure of the main rainy season

    The semi-arid sertao has among the clearest El Niño drought signals anywhere in the Americas.

    Exposure Subsistence agriculture and municipal water supply in a region with thin storage margins.

  • likelySouthern Brazil, Uruguay, northeast ArgentinaNov 2026–Feb 2027, under way
    Above-average rainfall and flooding

    A strengthened subtropical jet steers storms across the Plata basin.

    Exposure Soy and maize - beneficial in moderation, then damaging - and displacement along the Parana and Uruguay rivers.

  • likelyCoastal Peru and EcuadorDec 2026–Apr 2027, ahead
    Extreme coastal rainfall, flooding and debris flows

    The original El Niño. Requires warmth in Niño 1+2 specifically, which is why it is gated to east-Pacific events; a central-Pacific event of the same Niño 3.4 strength may produce very little of it.

    Exposure Huaicos destroying road and bridge links, urban flooding in Piura and Trujillo, and a sharp rise in waterborne disease.

    Reinforced by the east-Pacific flavour of this event.

  • likelyPeruvian anchoveta fisheryNov 2026–May 2027, under way
    Thermocline deepens and the fishery collapses

    Upwelling continues but draws warm nutrient-poor water; biomass falls and seasons are cancelled.

    Exposure The world's largest single-species fishery and the fishmeal supply underpinning global aquaculture and livestock feed prices.

    Reinforced by the east-Pacific flavour of this event.

North America

  • likelyUS Gulf Coast and SoutheastDec 2026–Mar 2027, ahead
    Wetter and stormier than normal

    A southward-displaced, strengthened subtropical jet. Also raises the cool-season tornado and severe-storm count across the Gulf states.

    Exposure Flood risk in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and Florida.

  • likelyCanada and the northern United StatesDec 2026–Feb 2027, ahead
    Milder winter

    A well-reproduced Pacific-North American pattern response.

    Exposure Lower heating demand, and a shorter ice season on the Great Lakes.

  • likelyUS Pacific Northwest and Ohio ValleyDec 2026–Mar 2027, ahead
    Drier and milder than normal

    The northern storm track lifts away, leaving a thin snowpack.

    Exposure Snowpack-dependent summer water supply and the following fire season.

  • likelyCalifornia and the US SouthwestDec 2026–Mar 2027, ahead
    Tilt toward a wetter winter, strongest in the south

    Less reliable than its reputation: several strong events delivered near-normal California precipitation. Southern California and Arizona have the clearer signal; northern California does not.

    Exposure Atmospheric-river flooding, debris flows on recent burn scars, and reservoir and snowpack recovery.

Global systems

  • likelyPacific island statesNov 2026–Apr 2027, under way
    Rainfall redistribution and a shifted cyclone belt

    Kiribati and Tuvalu turn wet while Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa and Papua New Guinea dry; the cyclone belt shifts east toward French Polynesia.

    Exposure Freshwater lenses on atolls, which fail before anything else does.

  • likelyPacific and Indian Ocean coral reefsDec 2026–Jun 2027, ahead
    Mass bleaching from accumulated heat stress

    The 1997-98, 2014-17 and 2023-25 events drove global bleaching episodes; the last put more than four fifths of the world's reef area under bleaching-level heat stress, the most extensive on record. Central and eastern Pacific reefs go first, then the wider basin.

    Exposure Reef fisheries, coastal protection from wave energy, and ecosystems that need a decade or more to recover if they recover at all.

  • likelyGlobal mean surface temperatureDec 2026–Nov 2027, ahead
    Elevated for roughly a year, peaking after the event

    Heat released from the Pacific raises global temperature with a lag of three to six months, so the warmest calendar year is usually the one AFTER the peak.

    Exposure Compounding with the background trend: the hottest years on record have been El Niño years riding on top of it.

  • likelyWestern North Pacific typhoonsAug–Dec 2026, under way
    Formation shifts southeast; longer, more intense tracks

    Genesis moves toward the southeast quadrant, giving storms a longer run over warm water and more time to intensify before recurving.

    Exposure Higher-intensity landfalls in Japan and Korea; more recurvature away from the Philippines even as that country dries.

  • likelyAtlantic hurricane seasonAug–Oct 2026, past
    Suppressed activity

    Increased vertical wind shear over the main development region. One of the most reliable seasonal-forecast signals in existence, and the clearest case where an El Niño reduces rather than increases a hazard.

    Exposure Fewer US and Caribbean landfalls - though a single storm in a quiet season still does what a single storm does.

    Reinforced by the east-Pacific flavour of this event.

  • likelyEastern and central Pacific hurricanesJul–Oct 2026, past
    Enhanced activity, tracking further west

    Warm water and reduced shear extend the basin westward, raising the risk to Hawaii and to central Pacific island states.

    Exposure Small island states with minimal margin for a direct strike.

Central America

  • likelyCaribbeanDec 2026–Apr 2027, ahead
    Drier than normal dry season

    Follows a suppressed Atlantic hurricane season, so two dry inputs arrive back to back.

    Exposure Island water supply with limited storage, and tourism-season demand.

  • likelyCentral American Dry CorridorMay–Aug 2026, past
    Delayed onset and mid-summer drought

    Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua. The canicula lengthens and the primera harvest fails.

    Exposure Smallholder maize and beans; repeated failures here are a documented driver of displacement and northward migration.

Southeast Asia

  • likelyMekong basin and ThailandNov 2026–May 2027, under way
    Reduced river flow and dry-season water stress

    Low wet-season accumulation carries into the dry season; compounded by upstream storage operations, which makes attribution to ENSO alone unsafe.

    Exposure Irrigated rice in the delta, salinity intrusion, and inland fisheries.

On watch — below the outlook’s bar at this peak

  • India and Pakistan — Weaker summer monsoon (contested: rated possible at most, however strong the event)

Momentum and coupling

Coupling is what turns a warm ocean into global teleconnections; without a Walker-circulation response the anomaly stays local.
